title: General design of enzymes for new chemical reactions

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a reliable way to turn a specified chemical reaction into an efficient, selective enzyme across a broad range of chemically different transformations. A researcher would specify the starting molecules, desired products and operating conditions, and the workflow would develop a protein catalyst with useful performance while keeping experimental screening within a defined budget. The ambition includes reactions without known enzymatic solutions; it does not require success for every conceivable reaction.

In the concept's scientific framing, this requires solving two connected design problems: identifying catalytic chemistry that can accelerate the desired transformation, and constructing a protein environment that makes that chemistry work. Arranging an established catalytic motif inside a new protein addresses an important part of the second problem. A broadly general workflow would also need to handle unfamiliar catalytic requirements, rather than depend entirely on arrangements already known to work. These distinctions describe the proposed capability; the supplied evidence does not establish that it has been achieved.

significance.text: If achieved, reliable reaction-to-enzyme design would make biocatalysis more programmable. Researchers could approach a new transformation through a reusable design workflow instead of beginning a large, bespoke laboratory evolution campaign each time. The direct advance would be greater predictability and broader access to selective catalysts, with experimental work serving validation and bounded refinement rather than an open-ended search. This is a conditional impact argument drawn from the proposed capability.

Cheaper manufacture of medicines and materials is a plausible downstream possibility, but an effective enzyme alone would not establish an economical process. Benefits would depend on feedstocks, enzyme production, operating conditions, competing reactions, product recovery and scale-up. The analogy to programming therefore has limits: specifying a desired reaction does not guarantee that a physically feasible catalyst exists, and a catalyst that works in a laboratory assay may still be unsuitable for manufacturing.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is dependable joint design of catalytic chemistry and a compatible protein across unfamiliar transformations. The research describes existing methods as insufficiently reliable for that goal, but the retained scientific evidence does not establish the extent of the limitation or its continuing scope. The substantive research question remains how to move from success on selected reaction families to a workflow whose performance transfers predictably across diverse chemistry.

The proposed problem involves several coupled physical requirements. A design must favor the desired reaction pathway and its transition states, position the relevant chemical groups, and accommodate protein motion and solvent effects. It must also suppress competing reactions sufficiently to deliver useful selectivity. A plausible static arrangement is therefore only part of the problem: the surrounding protein and reaction conditions must sustain productive chemistry. This is an explanatory synthesis of the supplied research framing, rather than a technical finding verified from the retained source.

A practical breakthrough would also require predicting which designs will work well enough to avoid extensive screening. Generality would be weakened if every unfamiliar reaction required expert invention of its catalytic arrangement or a large new evolution campaign. Conversely, some experimental refinement can fit the concept if its budget and role are defined in advance. The central engineering challenge is reliable performance with bounded iteration, alongside a clear account of where the workflow fails.

current_state.text: The supplied research identifies a paper as “Computational enzyme design by catalytic motif scaffolding,” attributes it to Markus Braun and colleagues, and gives a publication date of 3 December 2025 and DOI 10.1038/s41586-025-09747-9. It reports catalysts for two reaction classes, with some activities comparable to catalysts improved by laboratory evolution. These bibliographic and scientific details remain unverified here: according to the supplied review, the retained copy at the linked PubMed address contains only a cookie-related access message, without an abstract or article text. The link identifies the intended source, but the retained content cannot substantiate the reported results.

The research interprets that work as building protein scaffolds around established catalytic arrangements. If confirmed, this would demonstrate a narrower capability than general invention of active-site chemistry: successfully hosting a known catalytic arrangement does not by itself show that a workflow can discover suitable chemistry for unfamiliar reactions. Likewise, activity comparable to selected laboratory-evolved catalysts would require context about the reactions, assay conditions and comparison set before supporting a broader performance claim. Those details cannot be checked from the retained source.

The earlier research also refers to an accessible bibliographic record, a first-pass reading, and failed attempts to open the publisher page and PDF. The supplied review found no preserved material documenting those readings or access attempts, so they cannot serve as additional verification. The documented limitation is the cookie-only retained artifact. Missing article content does not show that the reported results are false, but it prevents a firm account of what was demonstrated. The supplied materials also do not establish comprehensive coverage through 1 November 2026 or whether the broader capability remained open at that date.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: evaluate one workflow on a preregistered, independently selected panel of chemically diverse reactions, including transformations without known enzymatic solutions. Before testing, define reaction-specific activity and selectivity thresholds, the allowed experimental screening budget, and the panel success rate required for a convincing result. These would be proposed evaluation choices, not established standards. The panel should make clear which catalytic requirements are supplied to the workflow and which it must derive.
completion_criteria.label: Diverse reaction panel meets preregistered success thresholds within screening budget

completion_criteria.text: Independent laboratories should reproduce several successful designs under predefined, realistic conditions. Reports should document experimental iteration, failed designs and assay conditions so that apparent generality cannot be explained by unreported screening or unusually favorable comparisons. Performance should be judged against the intended use: a useful research catalyst and a useful manufacturing catalyst may face different requirements for activity, selectivity, stability and operating conditions. This is a proposed reproducibility and practicality framework.
completion_criteria.label: Independent laboratories reproduce successful designs under realistic, use-specific conditions

completion_criteria.text: A convincing outcome would establish demonstrated breadth within a stated chemical and operational domain. It should distinguish reuse of established catalytic motifs from cases in which the workflow derives unfamiliar catalytic arrangements, and identify reactions or conditions outside its reliable range. A finite panel cannot establish literal universality; its value is evidence that the same method transfers across meaningfully different challenges with a bounded experimental burden.
completion_criteria.label: Chemical and operational breadth is demonstrated with stated reliability limits

related_concepts.text: BCH-02, “Predict biochemical function from molecular sequence and environment,” overlaps through the need to connect protein sequence and operating conditions to catalytic behavior. The distinction is between prediction and construction: BCH-02 asks what a molecular system will do, while BCH-01 asks how to create a catalyst for a chosen transformation. Accurate prediction could support enzyme design without itself delivering a working design workflow. This comparison is a synthesis based on the supplied roster.

BCH-03, “A self-maintaining, evolvable cell assembled from defined components,” could benefit from designed enzymes that supply missing reactions, but cellular maintenance and evolution require coordinated systems beyond an individual catalyst. BCH-04, “A chemically plausible route from simple feedstocks to evolving heredity,” concerns the emergence of heredity; deliberately engineered enzymes would not by themselves establish a chemically plausible origin pathway. BCH-07, “Autonomous heredity in a chemically distinct genetic polymer,” could intersect with enzymes that synthesize or process alternative polymers, while autonomous information inheritance remains a separate achievement. These are conceptual relationships inferred from the roster.

BCH-08, “Resolve the nitrogenase reaction cycle during nitrogen fixation,” shares the challenge of understanding catalytic chemistry. Resolving that particular mechanism could inform catalyst design, but mechanistic understanding of one enzyme and general design across reaction classes are distinct goals. BCH-09, “Predict and control the biochemical organization of condensates,” and BCH-10, “Predict modification-dependent biochemical networks,” concern environmental organization and interacting biochemical processes that could affect a designed enzyme's behavior. Success in an isolated reaction would not establish control over those larger systems. This is a roster-based comparison.

BCH-05, “Routine, comprehensive single-cell proteoform reading,” BCH-06, “A multiplexed biochemical flight recorder for living cells,” and BCH-11, “Routine structural reading of complex glycans,” concern measurement capabilities that could help characterize enzymes, cellular responses or reaction products in relevant applications. Their core achievements remain distinct: reading protein variants, recording cellular events and resolving glycan structures do not themselves provide a general route to designing catalytic chemistry. These possible connections are synthesis rather than demonstrated dependencies.

unresolved_issues: The intended paper's identity, publication date, reaction classes, activity measurements and comparison conditions need confirmation from inspectable bibliographic and scientific content.
The interpretation that the reported work scaffolds established catalytic arrangements, and its implications for inventing active-site chemistry, require checking against the full paper.
No preserved first-pass reading or publisher/PDF access record is supplied; their contents and access history remain unknown.
The supplied evidence does not establish field-wide progress through 1 November 2026 or the continuing scope of the general design problem.
The proposed evaluation still requires an actual reaction panel, numerical performance thresholds, screening budget, success rate and reproduction conditions.
